blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron using cathode ray experiments and proposed the Plum Pudding model.
Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment established the presence of a dense, positively charged nucleus.
Neils Bohr proposed quantized energy shells (K, L, M, N) to explain atomic stability.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron, a uncharged particle situated within the atomic nucleus.
Atomic Number (Z) represents total protons, while Mass Number (A) is the sum of protons and neutrons.

blocks.content:
All matter in the universe is made up of tiny particles called atoms.

An atom is the smallest unit of an element that takes part in chemical reactions.

Earlier, scientists believed that atoms were indivisible.

Later, experiments proved that atoms are made up of even smaller particles.
2. DISCOVERY OF SUB-ATOMIC PARTICLES

Scientists discovered that atoms are made up of three smaller particles called:

• Electrons

• Protons

• Neutrons

These particles are called sub-atomic particles.
2.1 ELECTRON

Electron was discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897.

Electrons are negatively charged particles.

They revolve around the nucleus of an atom.

Properties of electrons:

• Charge = Negative

• Mass = Very small

• Present outside the nucleus
2.2 PROTON

Proton was discovered by E. Goldstein.

Protons are positively charged particles.

They are present inside the nucleus of an atom.



Properties of protons:

• Charge = Positive

• Mass = Almost equal to neutron

• Present in nucleus
2.3 NEUTRON

Neutron was discovered by James Chadwick.

Neutrons have no charge.

They are also present inside the nucleus.

Properties of neutrons:

• Charge = Neutral

• Mass = Nearly equal to proton

• Present in nucleus
3. ATOMIC MODELS

Scientists proposed different models to explain the structure of the atom.

Important atomic models are:

• Thomson’s model

• Rutherford’s model

• Bohr’s model
3.1 THOMSON’S ATOMIC MODEL
J.J. Thomson proposed this model.

According to this model:

• Atom is a positively charged sphere.

• Electrons are embedded in it like plums in a pudding.



This model is called the Plum Pudding Model.

Limitation:

It could not explain the scattering of alpha particles.
3.2 RUTHERFORD’S ATOMIC MODEL

Rutherford performed the gold foil experiment.

Observations:

• Most alpha particles passed straight through.

• Some were deflected.

• Very few bounced back.

Conclusions:

• Atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

• Most of the atom is empty space.

• Electrons revolve around the nucleus.



Limitation:

This model could not explain stability of atom.
3.3 BOHR’S ATOMIC MODEL

Niels Bohr improved Rutherford’s model.

According to Bohr:

• Electrons revolve in fixed energy levels.

• These orbits are called shells.

• Energy is not radiated when electrons move in shells.
• Energy is absorbed or released when electrons jump between shells.
4. ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATION

Electrons are arranged in different shells around the nucleus.

The shells are named as:

K, L, M, N

Maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by formula:

2n²

Where n = shell number
5. VALENCY
An atom consists of a positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons revolving in discrete energy orbits.

Valency is the combining capacity of an atom.

It depends on the number of electrons present in the outermost shell.

If outer shell has:

• 1, 2 or 3 electrons → valency = same number

• 4 electrons → valency = 4

• 5, 6 or 7 electrons → valency = 8 – number of electrons
• 8 electrons → valency = 0
6. ATOMIC NUMBER

Atomic number is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom.

Atomic number = Number of protons = Number of electrons (in neutral atom)

7. MASS NUMBER

Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus.

Mass number = Number of protons + Number of neutrons
8. ISOTOPES

Isotopes are atoms of the same element having same atomic number but different mass number.

Examples:

• Hydrogen – Protium, Deuterium, Tritium

Uses of isotopes:

• Cobalt-60 in cancer treatment

• Iodine-131 in thyroid treatment

9. ISOBARS

Isobars are atoms of different elements having same mass number but different atomic numbers.

Example:

Calcium (20,40) and Argon (18,40)

CHAPTER 5 : CHEMICAL REACTIONS AND EQUATIONS
1. INTRODUCTION TO CHEMICAL REACTIONS

In our daily life, many changes take place around us.

Some changes are physical in nature, while some are chemical in nature.

A chemical reaction is a process in which one or more substances react together and form new substances.

These new substances have different properties from the original substances.

The substances that take part in a chemical reaction are called reactants.

The substances that are formed as a result of the reaction are called products.

2. CHEMICAL EQUATION

A chemical equation is a way of representing a chemical reaction using symbols and formulas.

It shows which substances are reacting and what substances are formed.

In a chemical equation:

• Reactants are written on the left-hand side.

• Products are written on the right-hand side.

• An arrow shows the direction of the reaction.

Example:

Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium Oxide
3. BALANCED CHEMICAL EQUATION

A chemical equation is said to be balanced when the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the equation.

This is based on the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

Therefore, during a chemical reaction, the total mass of reactants is always equal to the total mass of products.

Step 1: Write the word equation.

Step 2: Convert the word equation into a skeletal chemical equation.

Step 3: Balance the atoms of each element one by one.

Step 4: Check whether the number of atoms on both sides is equal.

Step 5: Write the final balanced chemical equation.
5. TYPES OF CHEMICAL REACTIONS

Chemical reactions are classified into different types based on the way they occur.

The main types of chemical reactions are described below.

5.1 COMBINATION REACTION

A combination reaction is a reaction in which two or more substances combine together to form a single product.

In this type of reaction, multiple reactants form only one product.

Example:

Calcium oxide + Water → Calcium hydroxide

This reaction releases heat, so it is also called an exothermic reaction.
5.2 DECOMPOSITION REACTION

A decomposition reaction is a reaction in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

This type of reaction usually requires energy in the form of heat, electricity or light.

Example:

Calcium carbonate → Calcium oxide + Carbon dioxide

This reaction occurs when calcium carbonate is heated.
5.3 DISPLACEMENT REACTION

A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.

Example:

Zinc + Copper sulphate → Zinc sulphate + Copper

In this reaction, zinc displaces copper because zinc is more reactive than copper.
5.4 DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT REACTION

In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds.

Example:

Sodium sulphate + Barium chloride → Barium sulphate + Sodium chloride

This type of reaction often results in the formation of a precipitate.
6. OXIDATION AND REDUCTION

Oxidation is the process in which a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen.

Reduction is the process in which a substance loses oxygen or gains hydrogen.

Oxidation and reduction always occur together.

That is why these reactions are called redox reactions.

Corrosion is the slow destruction of metals due to their reaction with air, moisture or chemicals.

The most common example of corrosion is rusting of iron.



Rusting occurs when iron reacts with oxygen and water to form rust.

Rust weakens the metal and causes damage.

Corrosion can be prevented by the following methods:

• Painting the metal surface

• Oiling or greasing the metal

• Galvanization (coating with zinc)

• Electroplating

• Making alloys

Rancidity is the process in which fats and oils present in food get oxidized and produce an unpleasant smell and taste.

It spoils the quality of food and makes it unfit for consumption.

Rancidity can be prevented by:

• Keeping food in airtight containers

• Refrigeration

• Adding antioxidants
10. IMPORTANT EXAM POINTS

• Chemical reactions produce new substances.

• Balanced equations follow law of conservation of mass.

• Rusting is an example of oxidation.

• Combination reactions form a single product.

• Rancidity spoils food items.
11. QUICK REVISION

• Chemical equations represent reactions.

• Oxidation and reduction occur together.

• Corrosion damages metals.

• Rancidity causes food spoilage.
